regions.name: Riverina
regions.blurb: The Riverina runs from the Murrumbidgee irrigation country around Griffith and Leeton down to the Murray at Albury. Wagga Wagga is the largest inland city in NSW and holds the Army recruit base at Kapooka plus a Charles Sturt University campus. The economy is rice, wine, canola, sheep, beef and food processing, with heavy freight moving on the Olympic Highway and the Sydney to Melbourne rail line.

regions.name: Murray
regions.blurb: The Murray region follows the river border from Corowa west through Deniliquin to Balranald. Almost every town here has a Victorian twin across the water, so trade, sport and tradie work cross the bridge daily. Rice, dairy, irrigated cropping and river tourism carry the economy, and water allocation decisions set the mood of every season.

regions.name: Hume and South West Slopes
regions.blurb: The South West Slopes climb from the Murrumbidgee at Gundagai up into the Snowy Valleys around Tumut and Tumbarumba. Softwood plantations, apples at Batlow, cherries at Young and fine wool run the district. The Hume Highway splits it in two, which is why Gundagai grew as a stopping town and why the bypass changed what its main street sells.

regions.name: Central West
regions.blurb: The Central West covers the tablelands and slopes from Bathurst and Orange out to Parkes and Forbes. Orange runs on cool climate wine, orchards and the Cadia gold mine. Bathurst has Charles Sturt University and the Mount Panorama circuit. West of them the country flattens into wheat, sheep and the Parkes freight hub on the inland rail alignment.

regions.name: Orana
regions.blurb: Orana takes in Dubbo and the plains north and west of it, out past Nyngan, Cobar and Bourke. Dubbo is the service centre for a third of the state, with a base hospital, the Taronga Western Plains Zoo and a large saleyard and freight trade. Beyond it the work is sheep, cattle, cotton on the Macquarie and copper and gold mining at Cobar.

regions.name: New England North West
regions.blurb: New England North West runs from the Liverpool Plains at Gunnedah up through Tamworth and Armidale to the granite country at Glen Innes and Tenterfield. Tamworth is the country music town and a major beef and poultry processing centre. Armidale has the University of New England. West on the flats, Moree and Narrabri grow cotton and grain, and the Australia Telescope Compact Array sits outside Narrabri.

regions.name: Northern Rivers
regions.blurb: The Northern Rivers stretch from the Clarence at Grafton up to the Queensland border at Tweed Heads. Byron Bay and Ballina take the visitors, Lismore is the regional service centre, and Casino carries beef processing. The 2022 floods reshaped the property market, the insurance picture and the building rules across the whole catchment.

regions.name: Mid North Coast
regions.blurb: The Mid North Coast runs from Forster and Taree north through Port Macquarie and Kempsey to Coffs Harbour. Health care and aged care are the biggest employers, followed by construction, tourism and banana and blueberry growing behind Coffs. Finishing the Pacific Highway duplication cut hours off the Sydney run and changed where people build.

regions.name: Hunter
regions.blurb: The Hunter takes in Newcastle, the Maitland and Cessnock valley towns, and the coal country up to Muswellbrook and Scone. Newcastle is the second largest city in NSW and its port moves more coal than any other port in the world. Thoroughbred studs sit around Scone, vineyards around Pokolbin, and the whole valley is arguing about what replaces mining.

regions.name: Central Coast
regions.blurb: The Central Coast sits between the Hawkesbury and Lake Macquarie, with Gosford and Wyong as its two centres. A large share of working residents commutes to Sydney on the M1 or the Central Coast and Newcastle rail line. Health, retail, construction and holiday trade around Terrigal and The Entrance make up most local jobs.

regions.name: Illawarra and South Coast
regions.blurb: This region runs from Wollongong and the escarpment suburbs south through Nowra and Batemans Bay to Eden near the Victorian border. Wollongong has the Port Kembla steelworks and the University of Wollongong. South of Kiama it turns into dairy, oysters, fishing and holiday towns that triple in size over January. The 2019 and 2020 fires burnt through much of the Shoalhaven and Eurobodalla and the rebuild is still visible.

regions.name: Southern Tablelands and Capital Country
regions.blurb: The Southern Tablelands cover Goulburn, Yass and Crookwell, the Southern Highlands towns, and Queanbeyan on the ACT border. Queanbeyan works as a Canberra suburb in everything but postcode, so trades there price against ACT rates and hold NSW licences. Sheep, cattle, wind farms around Crookwell and cool climate wine near Bowral make up the rest.

regions.name: Snowy Monaro
regions.blurb: Snowy Monaro runs from Cooma across the high treeless plains to Jindabyne, Berridale and Bombala. Winter is the business, with Perisher and Thredbo pulling traffic up the Kosciuszko Road and the Alpine Way from June to October. Snowy 2.0 construction has put hard pressure on housing and on every trade in the district.

regions.name: Far West
regions.blurb: The Far West is Broken Hill, Wentworth, Menindee and the country out to the South Australian and Queensland borders. Broken Hill has mined silver, lead and zinc since 1883 and runs on South Australian clock time rather than Sydney time. Distance is the defining fact here. Mildura is closer to Wentworth than any NSW centre of size.

regions.name: Blue Mountains
regions.blurb: The Blue Mountains climb from Glenbrook to Blackheath along the Great Western Highway, with Katoomba as the main centre and Lithgow at the western foot. Tourism at Echo Point and the Three Sisters drives the retail strip, while a large share of residents commute to Sydney by train. Building work here deals with bushfire attack level ratings and steep block access as a matter of course.

regions.name: Sydney Metro
regions.blurb: Sydney Metro covers the harbour city and the western centres at Parramatta, Blacktown, Liverpool, Penrith and Campbelltown. Parramatta is the second CBD and has taken most of the state government office relocation. For a directory the metro matters as the demand source, because a large share of the holiday and second home money spent in the regions starts here.

localities.name: Albury
localities.blurb: Albury sits on the NSW bank of the Murray with Dean Street as its retail spine and QEII Square at the centre of it. It works as one economy with Wodonga across the bridge, which is why so many trades here hold licences in both NSW and Victoria. Health, freight and the Ettamogah rail hub north of town carry most of the employment.

localities.name: Lavington
localities.blurb: Lavington is Albury's largest suburb and its trade counter belt, with Wagga Road running north to the Hume and Urana Road cutting west. Most of the north side buys tyres, timber and plumbing supplies here rather than driving into the city. It has its own shopping centre, a large sports club on Urana Road and a greyhound track.

localities.name: Thurgoona
localities.blurb: Thurgoona is the growth edge of Albury, built around a Charles Sturt University campus, a golf resort and a small shopping plaza. New estates keep pushing towards Table Top, so the work here is slabs, fencing, landscaping and split system installs rather than heritage repair. Nearly everyone drives into Albury or Lavington for anything beyond groceries.

localities.name: Jindera
localities.blurb: Jindera is 15 kilometres north of Albury and has grown fast as Albury workers buy land with room for a shed. The Pioneer Museum on Urana Street records the German Lutheran families who settled the district in the 1870s. Cropping and sheep country starts at the edge of the last estate.

localities.name: Table Top
localities.blurb: Table Top is a spread of rural blocks between Albury and Lake Hume, sitting under the flat topped hill it is named for. There is a public school and a hall and little else, so residents shop in Thurgoona or Lavington. Local jobs are rural fencing, septic systems, bore pumps and driveway grading.

localities.name: Bowna
localities.blurb: Bowna sits on the eastern arm of Lake Hume where the Murray Valley Highway leaves the Hume Freeway. The original village went under when the weir filled, so what is left is grazing land, lake frontage and the old cemetery on the hill. Boat ramps and holiday shacks mean seasonal demand for trailer repairs, pumps and caravan servicing.

localities.name: Gerogery
localities.blurb: Gerogery is a rail village north of Jindera with a store, a hotel and a primary school. The main southern line runs straight through it and the granite hills to the east draw weekend riders and shooters. Blocks around town are hobby farms and horse property, so stock fencing, sheds and tank installs are the common jobs.

localities.name: Burrumbuttock
localities.blurb: Burrumbuttock is 30 kilometres north west of Albury in mixed cropping and sheep country. It is best known outside the district for the Burrumbuttock hay runs, where convoys of donated fodder left from here for drought hit graziers in Queensland and western NSW. Anything beyond the hall and the school comes out of Jindera or Walla Walla.

localities.name: Walla Walla
localities.blurb: Walla Walla was settled in 1868 by German Lutheran families who drove their stock overland from South Australia, and the Lutheran church still anchors the town. It runs an annual show, keeps a bakery and a hotel going, and fields a footy side well above its weight. A large stockfeed and cropping trade gives the town more work than its size suggests.

localities.name: Culcairn
localities.blurb: Culcairn sits on the Olympic Highway and the main southern railway, and its two storey 1890s hotel with the deep verandah is the landmark on Balfour Street. The town services broadacre cropping and has a small industrial strip near the silos. Billabong Creek runs west of town and puts water over the flats in a big year.

localities.name: Henty
localities.blurb: Henty hosts the Henty Machinery Field Days each September, which puts tens of thousands of people and several hundred exhibitors into a paddock south of town. The header harvester was invented here in 1914 and the district still carries a serious agricultural engineering trade because of it. Wheat, canola and lupins dominate the surrounding country.

localities.name: Holbrook
localities.blurb: Holbrook has a submarine in a park beside the highway, which is odd for a town roughly 350 kilometres from the sea and exactly why people stop. The Hume bypass opened in 2013 and took the through traffic, so the main street rebuilt around the submarine park, the bakery trade and local services. Fine wool and cattle country runs east into the hills.

localities.name: Woomargama
localities.blurb: Woomargama is a village on the old Hume alignment between Holbrook and Albury, with Woomargama National Park rising behind it. The 2013 bypass pulled the traffic off the main street, so the hotel and hall now serve locals and park visitors. Work here is rural fencing, firewood, bushfire clearing and rural water supply.

localities.name: Mullengandra
localities.blurb: Mullengandra is a roadside locality south of Holbrook with a hall, a rest area and a creek of the same name. Almost all of it is grazing country running back into the hills towards Jingellic and the upper Murray. Residents use Holbrook or Albury for anything past fuel and a phone call.

localities.name: Wagga Wagga
localities.blurb: Wagga Wagga is the largest inland city in NSW, sitting on the Murrumbidgee with Baylis Street running down to the river and Wagga Beach. The Army recruit training centre at Kapooka and RAAF Base Wagga make defence a major employer alongside health and Charles Sturt University. Bomen, north east of the city, holds the abattoir and freight industry and keeps heavy trades busy.

localities.name: Lockhart
localities.blurb: Lockhart is called the Verandah Town because both sides of Green Street carry continuous iron lace awnings. It runs picnic races and a sculpture prize staged on a stubble paddock in spring. Wheat, canola and sheep are effectively the whole economy.

localities.name: The Rock
localities.blurb: The Rock takes its name from Kengal, the granite outcrop in the nature reserve just west of town, which has a walking track to the summit. The town sits on the Olympic Highway and the Wagga to Albury rail line, and plenty of residents drive to Wagga for work. Cropping, contract harvesting and a growing set of rural residential blocks make up the local trade.

localities.name: Uranquinty
localities.blurb: Uranquinty is 15 minutes south of Wagga on the Olympic Highway, built around a hotel, a hall and a primary school. It held a RAAF training airfield during the Second World War and the old base land still shapes the paddocks north of town. Most residents work in Wagga, so local demand is renovation, sheds and rural fencing.

localities.name: Junee
localities.blurb: Junee is a railway town. Its roundhouse is the largest surviving locomotive depot in NSW and still turns rolling stock, and the correctional centre on the edge of town is one of the biggest employers in the shire. Broadway is the main street, and a licorice and chocolate factory in an old flour mill pulls weekend traffic off the Olympic Highway.

localities.name: Coolamon
localities.blurb: Coolamon has a wide main street of intact Federation shopfronts and a preserved Edwardian department store kept as a museum. A cheese factory and solid cropping country give the town more trade than most places its size hold onto. Wagga is 40 minutes south east, which keeps the population steady.

localities.name: Ganmain
localities.blurb: Ganmain is known for hay. The district gave its name to a distinctive haystack build and still runs a hay carnival, and hay and straw contracting remains a real local industry. The town has a hotel, a bakery and a football ground, and Coolamon or Narrandera cover anything larger.

localities.name: Narrandera
localities.blurb: Narrandera sits where the Sturt and Newell Highways cross the Murrumbidgee, which makes it a natural overnight stop for trucks and caravans. Lake Talbot and its pool complex, plus the koala regeneration reserve, carry the visitor trade. Timber milling, cropping and highway business keep the town going.

localities.name: Leeton
localities.blurb: Leeton was laid out by Walter Burley Griffin, so the centre has curved streets and a circular civic layout that looks nothing like the usual Riverina grid. It is a food processing town, with rice and juice plants providing most of the wage jobs. Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area canals run through the farmland on every side.

localities.name: Griffith
localities.blurb: Griffith is the centre of the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area and produces more wine by volume than any other district in NSW. Italian families who arrived after both wars shaped the food, the citrus blocks and the vineyards, and Banna Avenue still shows it. Water allocation, freight and food processing set the tone of the local economy every year.

localities.name: Hay
localities.blurb: Hay sits on the Murrumbidgee in the middle of the Hay Plains, where the horizon is as flat as anywhere in the country. The Long Paddock stock route, a shearing museum and the preserved gaol carry the tourist trade, and the town is a fixed overnight stop on the Sturt Highway. Merino wool, fat lambs and irrigated cotton run the district.

localities.name: Temora
localities.blurb: Temora has an aviation museum with a flying collection of warbirds and an aerodrome that stages regular showcase days. The town grew on an 1880s gold rush and now runs on wheat, canola and sheep. Hoskins Street is the main strip and the rail line still moves grain out of the local silos.

localities.name: West Wyalong
localities.blurb: West Wyalong has a main street that bends because it followed a bullock track around the old mining leases. Gold is still worked nearby and the town sits where the Newell and Mid Western Highways meet, so heavy vehicle trade matters here. Wheat and canola country runs out in every direction.

localities.name: Corowa
localities.blurb: Corowa calls itself the birthplace of Federation because the 1893 conference that broke the deadlock was held here. The bridge over the Murray runs straight into Wahgunyah and the Rutherglen wine country, so trade crosses the border all day. Cropping, sheep, a flour mill and river tourism support the town.

localities.name: Howlong
localities.blurb: Howlong sits on the Murray halfway between Albury and Corowa, with its own bridge into Victoria and a large golf course beside the river. Retirees and Albury commuters have driven most of the growth in the last twenty years. The main street covers daily needs and Albury is 25 minutes east on the Riverina Highway.

localities.name: Mulwala
localities.blurb: Mulwala sits on the NSW side of Lake Mulwala, joined to Yarrawonga by the weir bridge. Boating, water skiing and the clubs carry the economy through summer, and holiday houses outnumber permanent homes in some streets. A government propellant factory north of town has been a steady industrial employer for decades.

localities.name: Urana
localities.blurb: Urana is a small town with a wide main street and a lake on its edge that fills in wet years and draws campers when it does. It lost its own shire in the 2016 council amalgamations and now sits inside Federation Council with Corowa. Sheep, wheat and the caravan park by the water are what remains of the trade.

localities.name: Berrigan
localities.blurb: Berrigan has a racecourse, a bowling club and grain silos on the rail line, and gives its name to the shire that also covers Finley, Tocumwal and Barooga. Council and school jobs matter more here than in most towns this size. The surrounding country runs sheep, wheat and irrigated pasture.

localities.name: Finley
localities.blurb: Finley sits where the Newell and Riverina Highways cross, which makes it the service stop for a large rice and cropping district. There is a lake and swimming complex on the southern edge and a working saleyard. Irrigation water allocation is the single biggest factor in how local business goes each year.

localities.name: Tocumwal
localities.blurb: Tocumwal has a wide sandy river beach on the Murray and a foreshore that fills with campers every summer. Its aerodrome was a major Second World War bomber base and is now one of the main gliding centres in the country. Tourism, cropping and river holiday homes carry the local economy.

localities.name: Barooga
localities.blurb: Barooga sits across the river from Cobram and shares the 3644 postcode with it, which tells you how tightly the two towns work as one. Golf and the club trade bring most of the visitors, and irrigated dairy and orchards surround the town. Anything the main street cannot supply is a five minute drive into Victoria.

localities.name: Jerilderie
localities.blurb: Jerilderie is remembered for the 1879 Kelly Gang raid, when the gang held the town for two days and left behind the letter that carries its name. It sits on the Newell Highway, so passing freight and grain trade keep the businesses on Jerilderie Street alive. Sheep, wheat and rice run the surrounding district.

localities.name: Deniliquin
localities.blurb: Deniliquin is the main centre of the southern Riverina rice country and once ran the largest rice mill in the southern hemisphere. The Edward River loops through the middle of town and the beach on the bend is used all summer. The ute muster each October brings tens of thousands of people and books out every trade and bed in town.

localities.name: Moama
localities.blurb: Moama is on the NSW bank opposite Echuca, joined by the bridge over the Murray. Its clubs, caravan parks and river frontage pull Victorian visitors and their money across the border constantly. New estates on the eastern edge have grown quickly because land here has been cheaper than the Echuca side.

localities.name: Barham
localities.blurb: Barham faces Koondrook across the Murray, joined by a lift span bridge that still raises for river traffic. Red gum timber, dairy and irrigated cropping built the town and timber work is still part of it. The riverfront caravan parks fill at Christmas and Easter and empty again by February.

localities.name: Balranald
localities.blurb: Balranald sits on the Murrumbidgee not far above its junction with the Murray, and it is the last real service town before the Hay Plains or Mildura. The turn off for Yanga National Park and the Mungo road is here, so tourism now sits alongside grazing and irrigated cropping. Fuel, tyres and mechanical work matter more than usual because of the distances.

localities.name: Moulamein
localities.blurb: Moulamein claims to be the oldest town in the Riverina, surveyed on the Edward River in the 1840s when paddle steamers still worked the run. It has a wharf reserve, a lake, a hotel and a grain receival site, and very little passing traffic. Rice, wheat and sheep are the local work, with Barham or Deniliquin for anything else.

localities.name: Tumbarumba
localities.blurb: Tumbarumba sits above 600 metres in the foothills of the Snowy Mountains and grows some of the coolest climate wine in NSW. Softwood plantations and the mills below town are the biggest employer, alongside beef and fine wool. The rail trail through to Rosewood was the first of its kind to open in NSW.

localities.name: Tumut
localities.blurb: Tumut sits in a valley below the Snowy scheme with the river running past the edge of the main street. Softwood processing is the largest employer in town, and Snowy 2.0 work has added contractors and squeezed the rental market. Wynyard Street is the retail strip and the trout season brings visitors from October.

localities.name: Batlow
localities.blurb: Batlow grows apples, and the orchards on the ridges around town supply a large share of the NSW crop. The cider festival each autumn is the town's biggest day of the year. The 2020 fires reached the town edge and cost growers trellis, netting and whole blocks, and that recovery is still visible.

localities.name: Adelong
localities.blurb: Adelong kept a main street of 1860s gold rush buildings, and the ruins of the crushing works still stand in the creek at Adelong Falls just above town. It sits a few minutes off the Snowy Mountains Highway between Gundagai and Tumut. Grazing, forestry and passing tourist trade keep it going.

localities.name: Gundagai
localities.blurb: Gundagai sits above the Murrumbidgee flats because the 1852 flood destroyed the original town on the low ground and killed most of its people. The Dog on the Tuckerbox is five kilometres north and the old timber viaduct still crosses the floodplain. Sheep, cattle and highway service trade support the town now that the Hume runs past it.

localities.name: Cootamundra
localities.blurb: Cootamundra is a rail junction town with a wide main street and the wattle that carries its name. Sir Donald Bradman was born here and the cottage is kept as a museum, which brings a steady trickle of visitors off the Olympic Highway. Wheat, canola, fat lambs and rail maintenance make up the local economy.

localities.name: Young
localities.blurb: Young calls itself the cherry capital of Australia and runs a cherry festival every December. The Lambing Flat riots of 1861 happened here and the museum in town records them plainly. Cherries, prunes, canola and sheep drive a labour market that spikes hard at harvest and needs housing for pickers.

localities.name: Harden
localities.blurb: Harden and Murrumburrah sit side by side, one built by the railway and the other by the road, and locals treat them as one town. The first Australian Horse regiment was raised at Murrumburrah in 1897 and there is a memorial and small museum to it. Grain, sheep and rail freight are the local work, with Cootamundra and Yass the nearest larger centres.

localities.name: Orange
localities.blurb: Orange sits at about 860 metres on the slopes of Mount Canobolas, which is why it grows cool climate wine and apples and gets frosts the rest of the Central West does not. The Cadia mine south of town is one of the largest gold operations in the country and underwrites a lot of local trade. Summer Street is the main strip and the food and wine trade is what brings Sydney visitors over the range.

localities.name: Bathurst
localities.blurb: Bathurst is the oldest inland European settlement in Australia, laid out on the Macquarie in 1815. Mount Panorama is a public road for most of the year and a racetrack for the rest, and the October race weekend loads every bed, kitchen and mechanic in the district. Charles Sturt University, the courts and the health service are the steady employers.

localities.name: Cowra
localities.blurb: Cowra is known for the 1944 breakout, when more than a thousand Japanese prisoners of war rushed the wire at the camp on the edge of town. The Japanese Garden built afterwards is the main visitor draw and the war cemetery is maintained here. Cropping, lucerne, vineyards and an abattoir carry the local economy.

localities.name: Forbes
localities.blurb: Forbes has a lake in the middle of town, a wide 1880s main street and a long relationship with the Lachlan River. It floods, and the 2022 events put water through town twice inside two months. Sheep, wheat, canola and Newell Highway freight are the working economy.

localities.name: Parkes
localities.blurb: Parkes has the radio telescope 20 kilometres north that carried the Apollo 11 television signal, and an Elvis festival each January that fills every bed in town. It sits where the Newell Highway crosses the main west rail line, which is why the national logistics hub was built here. Freight, farming and rail work drive employment.

localities.name: Mudgee
localities.blurb: Mudgee runs on wine, food and weekend traffic from Sydney, with cellar doors spread through the hills north of town. Coal mines at Ulan and Wilpinjong pay a large share of local wages and keep diesel fitters and fabricators busy. Church Street and the Saturday growers market carry the visitor trade.

localities.name: Blayney
localities.blurb: Blayney sits between Bathurst and Orange on the main west line, and the wind farm on the ridge above town was one of the first built in NSW. An abattoir and a dairy processing plant supply most of the wage jobs. It is high, cold country and the frost hollows around town are notorious.

localities.name: Dubbo
localities.blurb: Dubbo is the service centre for the western half of the state, with a base hospital, courts, government offices and one of the busiest saleyards in NSW. Taronga Western Plains Zoo is the visitor drawcard and the Macquarie runs through the middle of town. The airport carries heavy regional traffic and Newell Highway freight keeps transport and mechanical trades in constant work.

localities.name: Narromine
localities.blurb: Narromine sits on the Macquarie west of Dubbo and has a long gliding history, with its aerodrome hosting national and international competitions. Cotton, wheat and citrus grow on the irrigated country around it. The town works hand in hand with Dubbo, 40 kilometres east on the Mitchell Highway.

localities.name: Nyngan
localities.blurb: Nyngan sits on the Bogan River where the Mitchell and Barrier Highways meet, and the 1990 flood that forced the whole town to evacuate by helicopter is still the local reference point. A levee now rings the town. Sheep, wheat and the solar farm south of town are the main industry.

localities.name: Warren
localities.blurb: Warren sits on the Macquarie in cotton and merino country and trades hard on the quality of its wool clip. The Macquarie Marshes north west of town are a major wetland and bird breeding ground when the river runs. Irrigation allocation and gin work set the seasonal rhythm of local business.

localities.name: Coonabarabran
localities.blurb: Coonabarabran calls itself the astronomy capital of Australia because Siding Spring Observatory sits on the ridge above town in the Warrumbungles. The national park brings walkers and climbers year round and the dark sky rules affect local lighting choices. Timber, cattle and Newell Highway trade make up the rest of the economy.

localities.name: Cobar
localities.blurb: Cobar is a copper and gold town on the Barrier Highway where mining has run in one form or another since the 1870s. The heritage listed Great Cobar building holds the museum and the workings sit right on the edge of town. Mining wages set what housing and trade labour cost here, and they move with the copper price.

localities.name: Bourke
localities.blurb: Bourke sits on the Darling at the edge of the outback, and the phrase back of Bourke came from exactly this geography. Cotton, citrus and grazing depend on river water, and the old wharf and the exhibition centre carry what tourism there is. Dubbo is about four hours south east, which shapes how everything from freight to specialist trades is priced.

localities.name: Tamworth
localities.blurb: Tamworth runs the country music festival every January, which fills the town for ten days and books out motels an hour in every direction. Beef and poultry processing, a large equine centre and the regional hospital are the year round employers. Peel Street is the main strip and the Golden Guitar sits beside the New England Highway south of town.

localities.name: Armidale
localities.blurb: Armidale sits at about 980 metres on the New England Tablelands, so it gets genuine winter and the occasional snowfall. The University of New England and several large boarding schools mean the population swings with the academic year and rentals tighten every February. Fine wool, beef, health and education carry the economy.

localities.name: Inverell
localities.blurb: Inverell is called the Sapphire City because the country around it produced a large share of the world's commercial sapphire. Behind that sit silica sand, beef, cropping and a bigger engineering and manufacturing sector than most towns this size hold. Copeton Dam west of town is the local water supply and the summer holiday spot.

localities.name: Glen Innes
localities.blurb: Glen Innes leans on its Celtic heritage, with standing stones on the hill above town and an annual Australian Celtic Festival. It sits above 1000 metres on the New England Highway and wind farm construction nearby has brought in contractor work. Beef, sheep and forestry are the base industries.

localities.name: Moree
localities.blurb: Moree sits on the Mehi River in the middle of the northern cotton and grain country. Its artesian hot baths have drawn visitors since the 1890s and still bring caravans through every winter. Cotton gins, grain handling and Newell Highway freight are the main employers.

localities.name: Narrabri
localities.blurb: Narrabri is a cotton town on the Namoi with gins, grain silos and a rail line that moves both. The Australia Telescope Compact Array sits on the plain west of town and Mount Kaputar National Park rises to the east. Coal and gas projects nearby have been the biggest local argument for more than a decade.

localities.name: Gunnedah
localities.blurb: Gunnedah sits on the Liverpool Plains, some of the most productive cropping soil in the country, and calls itself the koala capital of the world. Coal mines and grain handling provide most of the wage jobs and the rail line carries both out. Conadilly Street is the main strip and the saleyards still matter to the town.

localities.name: Tenterfield
localities.blurb: Tenterfield sits at about 850 metres on the New England Highway, an hour south of the Queensland border. Henry Parkes gave the 1889 oration here that set Federation moving, and the School of Arts hall where he spoke still stands on Rouse Street. Grazing, forestry and highway trade carry the town, with Bald Rock National Park 30 kilometres north.

localities.name: Lismore
localities.blurb: Lismore sits in the Wilsons River flood plain and the February 2022 flood peaked above 14 metres, metres over the old record, and went through the CBD. Buybacks, raised rebuilds and insurance availability are still the dominant local issue. Southern Cross University, the base hospital and the beef and macadamia country around town carry the economy.

localities.name: Ballina
localities.blurb: Ballina sits at the mouth of the Richmond with a working prawn fleet and the regional airport that carries most Byron traffic. The big prawn on the old highway is the town joke that became a landmark. Retirement, health care, tourism and boat building make up most of the work.

localities.name: Byron Bay
localities.blurb: Byron Bay is the most easterly town in Australia and the Cape Byron lighthouse marks the point. Tourism is effectively the whole economy, and housing costs have pushed most of the workforce inland to Bangalow, Mullumbimby and Lismore. Trades here work around holiday letting turnover and tight development controls.

localities.name: Tweed Heads
localities.blurb: Tweed Heads runs straight into Coolangatta with the state border down the middle of a street, and a large share of the town shops in Queensland. Daylight saving makes trading hours a genuine problem for six months of the year. Retirement, health care, construction and the club trade drive the local economy.

localities.name: Casino
localities.blurb: Casino is a beef town with one of the largest meat processing works in NSW on its edge, and Beef Week each May is the event of the year. It sits where the Bruxner Highway meets the north coast rail line, so stock transport and freight matter here. The Richmond River runs past the showground end of town.

localities.name: Grafton
localities.blurb: Grafton turns purple every November when the jacarandas flower, and the festival built around it is the oldest floral festival in Australia. The old bascule bridge and the newer crossing set how traffic moves over the Clarence. Timber, beef, sugar and the correctional centre south of town are the main employers.

localities.name: Yamba
localities.blurb: Yamba sits at the mouth of the Clarence with a working fishing fleet, a surf beach and a fast growing retirement population. The breakwall walk and the ferry across to Iluka are the local fixtures. Building work here is holiday houses and unit blocks, and salt air corrosion drives a lot of the maintenance trade.

localities.name: Murwillumbah
localities.blurb: Murwillumbah sits inside the Tweed Valley caldera under Wollumbin, surrounded by cane, bananas and macadamias. The town took serious water in the 2022 flood and the main street is still working through it. The Tweed Valley Hospital 20 minutes north east has become a major regional employer.

localities.name: Port Macquarie
localities.blurb: Port Macquarie began as a convict settlement in 1821 and St Thomas church and the old courthouse still date from then. It now runs on health, aged care, construction and tourism, and the coastal walk from Town Beach out to Tacking Point lighthouse is what most visitors do first. The koala hospital is the best known institution in town.

localities.name: Coffs Harbour
localities.blurb: Coffs Harbour has the Big Banana, a jetty precinct and a harbour under Muttonbird Island, and a highway bypass that has kept the northern edge of town under construction for years. Blueberries have overtaken bananas as the main crop on the hills behind town. Health, education, tourism and berry farming carry the economy.

localities.name: Taree
localities.blurb: Taree sits on the Manning River about 20 minutes inland from Old Bar and Harrington. Health care and retail are now the biggest employers, since the Pacific Highway runs past the town rather than through it. Dairy, beef and estuary oysters are the traditional industries and the river still floods.

localities.name: Forster
localities.blurb: Forster and Tuncurry sit either side of the Wallis Lake entrance, joined by the bridge, and the oyster leases in the lake are the local signature. It is a retirement and holiday town, so the population swells over January and trade demand follows it. Fishing, tourism and aged care are the mainstays.

localities.name: Kempsey
localities.blurb: Kempsey sits on the Macleay River inland from Crescent Head and South West Rocks. It is dairy and beef country and the Akubra hat factory has been part of the town since the 1970s. The highway bypass took passing trade out of the main street and local retail has been adjusting to that ever since.

localities.name: Nambucca Heads
localities.blurb: Nambucca Heads sits where the Nambucca River meets the sea, and the V Wall breakwater covered in painted rocks is the landmark everyone photographs. Tourism, fishing and retirement money run the town. Macksville is ten minutes south and the two share most of the same service catchment.

localities.name: Wauchope
localities.blurb: Wauchope is 20 minutes inland from Port Macquarie on the Hastings River and was built on timber. Timbertown, a working heritage sawmill village, is the visitor attraction and the steam engine still runs. Cheaper land than the coast has made it a builder's town, with new estates spreading onto the ridges.

localities.name: Newcastle
localities.blurb: Newcastle is the second largest city in NSW and its port ships more coal than any other port in the world. The centre has been rebuilt since the steelworks closed, with light rail along Hunter Street and apartments on the old rail land at Honeysuckle. The University of Newcastle, the health service and the port are the biggest employers.

localities.name: Maitland
localities.blurb: Maitland sits on the Hunter River with High Street in Central Maitland as its heritage retail strip. It floods, and the 1955 flood is still the benchmark every local argument about levees comes back to. Growth at Rutherford and Thornton has been among the fastest in regional NSW, so residential construction drives most trade demand.

localities.name: Cessnock
localities.blurb: Cessnock is the working town at the door of the Hunter vineyards, with the Pokolbin cellar doors 15 minutes north west. Coal mining built it and hospitality now employs a large share of the town. Weekend weddings and functions in the vineyards keep accommodation, catering and hire trades busy year round.

localities.name: Singleton
localities.blurb: Singleton sits in the middle of the Hunter coal country with several large open cuts inside 20 minutes of town. The army training area at Singleton adds a second major employer. Mine wages set what local trades charge, and rentals move with shutdown and shift schedules.

localities.name: Muswellbrook
localities.blurb: Muswellbrook is a coal and power town, with Bayswater and the old Liddell site just south of it. Liddell shut down in 2023 and the district is openly working through what replaces those jobs. Thoroughbred studs and cattle country sit on the land away from the mines.

localities.name: Scone
localities.blurb: Scone calls itself the horse capital of Australia and the thoroughbred studs through the upper Hunter back the claim. The horse festival in May and the yearling sales bring serious money into town for short bursts. Farriers, equine vets, feed suppliers and horse transport are genuine local industries here.

localities.name: Nelson Bay
localities.blurb: Nelson Bay is the main town of Port Stephens, on a deep sheltered bay with dolphin cruises running out of the marina. Holiday letting drives the property market and the population multiplies over summer and Easter. Fishing, tourism and marine services are the local trades.

localities.name: Raymond Terrace
localities.blurb: Raymond Terrace sits where the Williams River meets the Hunter, just north of Newcastle and next door to the RAAF base and airport at Williamtown. Defence work and aviation contracting support a real engineering trade here. The highway now bypasses the old centre, which pushed retail out to the highway edge.

localities.name: Gosford
localities.blurb: Gosford sits at the head of Brisbane Water with the Sydney rail line running through the middle of it. Hospital and office development around the CBD has been the attempt to hold professional jobs on the coast rather than lose them to Sydney every morning. Kibble Park and the waterfront are the centre of town.

localities.name: Terrigal
localities.blurb: Terrigal has the beach, the Haven and the Skillion headland, and an esplanade that fills every weekend through summer. It is the most expensive stretch of the Central Coast and the property market makes that obvious. Hospitality, tourism and renovation work on the steep ridge streets are the local economy.

localities.name: Wyong
localities.blurb: Wyong sits on its own river at the northern end of the Central Coast, with both the M1 and the rail line running past. It holds more industrial and light manufacturing land than the Gosford end of the coast. The racecourse and the hospital at nearby Kanwal are the local anchors.

localities.name: The Entrance
localities.blurb: The Entrance sits on the channel between Tuggerah Lake and the sea, and the daily pelican feed on the foreshore is the event that pulls the crowd. Holiday units and caravan parks make it a summer town with a very quiet winter. Fishing, tourism and aged care carry the rest of the year.

localities.name: Wollongong
localities.blurb: Wollongong sits in a narrow strip between the escarpment and the sea, with the steelworks at Port Kembla still the largest industrial site in NSW. The University of Wollongong and the health service are the other major employers. Crown Street mall is the retail centre and the northern villages along Lawrence Hargrave Drive trade at Sydney prices.

localities.name: Shellharbour
localities.blurb: Shellharbour covers the old village on the point and the newer city centre inland, with the Bass Point quarry to the south. Estates at Flinders and Shell Cove have been among the fastest growing in the Illawarra and the Shell Cove marina is the newest piece of it. Most working residents drive into Wollongong or Port Kembla.

localities.name: Kiama
localities.blurb: Kiama is built around the blowhole on the headland and the harbour beside it. Dairy country climbs the escarpment behind town and the coast walk south to Gerringong brings day trippers off the train. Tourism, holiday letting and a large retiree population set the shape of local trade.

localities.name: Nowra
localities.blurb: Nowra and Bomaderry sit either side of the Shoalhaven River and work as a single town split by a bridge. HMAS Albatross, the naval air station west of town, is the biggest single employer in the district. Dairy, timber, Jervis Bay tourism and defence contracting carry the local economy.

localities.name: Ulladulla
localities.blurb: Ulladulla has a working harbour with a fishing fleet, and the Blessing of the Fleet at Easter is the oldest event on the town calendar. Milton sits five minutes north with its heritage main street and the two operate as one market. The 2019 fires burnt to the edge of both, which changed how people here think about clearing and access.

localities.name: Batemans Bay
localities.blurb: Batemans Bay sits at the mouth of the Clyde River, two hours from Canberra, and Canberra money dominates the holiday and property market. The 2020 fires cut the town off and burnt through much of the surrounding shire. Oysters, fishing, tourism and holiday house construction are the local industries.

localities.name: Moruya
localities.blurb: Moruya is the administrative centre of the Eurobodalla, with the council offices and the district hospital. Granite quarried here went into the pylons of the Sydney Harbour Bridge. Dairy, oysters, the Saturday markets on the river flat and the airstrip that serves the coast make up the local economy.

localities.name: Narooma
localities.blurb: Narooma sits on Wagonga Inlet with a boardwalk, a notorious bar crossing and Montague Island offshore. Island tours and the game fishing fleet drive most of the visitor trade. Oysters, tourism and a large retired population run the town the rest of the year.

localities.name: Bega
localities.blurb: Bega is the dairy centre of the far south coast and the cheese factory and its visitor centre are what the town is known for nationally. The hospital and the council make it the service town for the whole valley. The 2019 and 2020 fires burnt a large part of the district and the rebuild is still under way.

localities.name: Merimbula
localities.blurb: Merimbula sits on a lake and a sand bar, with the airport that connects the far south coast to Sydney and Melbourne. Oysters from the lake and holiday letting are the two constants in the local economy. The population roughly doubles in January, which is when most businesses here make their year.

localities.name: Eden
localities.blurb: Eden is a deep water port with a working fishing fleet and an extended wharf that takes cruise ships in season. The killer whale museum, built around the skeleton of Old Tom, is the local institution. Timber, fishing, port work and tourism are the industries, and the Victorian border is under an hour south.

localities.name: Goulburn
localities.blurb: Goulburn was the first inland city proclaimed in Australia and the Big Merino beside the highway tells you exactly what built it. The NSW Police Academy is a major employer, alongside the correctional centre and Hume Highway freight. Auburn Street is the main strip and the wind off the tablelands is a genuine design factor for anything built here.

localities.name: Queanbeyan
localities.blurb: Queanbeyan sits on the ACT border and works as a Canberra suburb with NSW rules, which matters for licensing, land price and stamp duty. The Queanbeyan River runs through the centre and has flooded the low streets more than once. Most residents work in Canberra, and local trades hold NSW licences while pricing against ACT rates.

localities.name: Yass
localities.blurb: Yass sits on the Hume 40 minutes north of Canberra and has become a commuter town because of it. Comur Street keeps a long heritage retail strip and the bypass keeps the trucks off it. Fine wool, cool climate wine and Canberra wages set the local market.

localities.name: Crookwell
localities.blurb: Crookwell sits above 800 metres in potato and fine wool country, and the wind farms on the ridges above town were among the first built in Australia. Cold climate crops and grazing are the base, with garden tourism bringing weekend visitors in spring and autumn. Goulburn is 40 minutes south east for anything the main street cannot cover.

localities.name: Bowral
localities.blurb: Bowral is the main town of the Southern Highlands, known for Tulip Time in September and the Bradman museum beside the oval. It has become a retirement and weekender town for Sydney money and the property market shows it plainly. Cafes, homewares, garden maintenance and high end renovation are the local trades.

localities.name: Moss Vale
localities.blurb: Moss Vale is the working town of the Southern Highlands, with the saleyards, the industrial estate and the rail junction to Unanderra. It trades on farm supply and services rather than tourism, which sets it apart from Bowral ten minutes north. Dairy, beef and a growing residential edge drive the local economy.

localities.name: Braidwood
localities.blurb: Braidwood was the first entire town in NSW to be heritage listed and every shopfront on Wallace Street reflects that. It sits on the Kings Highway between Canberra and Batemans Bay, so passing trade is a real part of the economy. Grazing, fine wool and a strong crafts and gallery trade carry the rest.

localities.name: Cooma
localities.blurb: Cooma was the headquarters of the Snowy Mountains Scheme, and the migrant workforce that built it left the town its Avenue of Flags and its clubs. It is the last large service stop before the mountains, so tyres, chains, fuel and mechanical work spike hard every winter. Snowy Hydro still has offices here and the Monaro grazing country covers the rest.

localities.name: Jindabyne
localities.blurb: Jindabyne sits on the lake that drowned the original town when the Snowy scheme dammed the river in the 1960s. It is the base for Perisher and Thredbo, so population, prices and staffing swing violently between winter and the shoulder seasons. Snowy 2.0 work has added pressure to a housing market that was already stretched.

localities.name: Berridale
localities.blurb: Berridale sits on the Monaro plains between Cooma and Jindabyne and calls itself the crossroads of the Snowy. Land is cheaper than Jindabyne, so a lot of resort staff and tradespeople live here and drive up the hill. Grazing, trout fishing on Lake Eucumbene and winter traffic make up the local trade.

localities.name: Bombala
localities.blurb: Bombala is timber country at the southern end of the Monaro, closer to Cann River in Victoria than to any large NSW centre. The platypus reserve on the river is the visitor draw and the mills are the employers. Fine wool, beef and forestry keep the town running.

localities.name: Adaminaby
localities.blurb: Adaminaby was moved uphill in the 1950s when Lake Eucumbene flooded the original site, and the old town reappears when the lake drops low enough. The Big Trout on the main street says what people come for. Trout fishing, grazing and trail riding carry the village through the year.

localities.name: Broken Hill
localities.blurb: Broken Hill has mined silver, lead and zinc since 1883 and the line of lode still runs along the ridge above the streets. The whole city is heritage listed, it keeps South Australian clock time, and Adelaide is closer than Sydney by a long way. Mining, film production and outback tourism through Silverton and the Menindee Lakes make up the economy.

localities.name: Wentworth
localities.blurb: Wentworth sits where the Darling meets the Murray, and the junction lookout is the reason most travellers stop. Locks, weirs and paddle steamer history define the town, and Mildura is 30 minutes west across the Victorian border. Irrigated horticulture, grazing and river tourism carry the trade.

localities.name: Menindee
localities.blurb: Menindee sits on the Darling below the lakes that hold water for Broken Hill. The mass fish deaths in the lower Darling in 2019 and again in 2023 put the town on national news, and river health is the constant local argument. Table grapes, citrus, grazing and lake tourism are the industries.

localities.name: Silverton
localities.blurb: Silverton is a near ghost town 25 kilometres from Broken Hill that has appeared in more films and commercials than most Australian cities. The hotel, the old gaol museum and the Mundi Mundi lookout are effectively the whole town. Film crews, tourists and a handful of resident artists keep it going.

localities.name: Katoomba
localities.blurb: Katoomba is the main town of the Blue Mountains, with Echo Point and the Three Sisters a short walk from the shops. Katoomba Street runs steeply downhill from the highway and holds most of the retail. Tourism is the biggest employer and a large share of residents still commute to Sydney by train.

localities.name: Blackheath
localities.blurb: Blackheath sits at the highest point of the Great Western Highway crossing, above 1000 metres, and gets snow most winters. Govetts Leap and the Grand Canyon track bring bushwalkers all year. Cafes, antiques and weekender houses make up a large part of the local trade.

localities.name: Springwood
localities.blurb: Springwood is the main centre of the lower mountains, with Macquarie Road as the retail strip and a heavy commuter population on the Sydney line. It is warmer and closer to Penrith than the upper mountains, which shapes who buys here. The 2013 fires burnt through Winmalee next door and bushfire attack level rules still drive local building work.

localities.name: Wentworth Falls
localities.blurb: Wentworth Falls takes its name from the waterfall at the end of the valley, and the Charles Darwin walk follows the creek down to the top of it. The village strip on the highway serves residents and walkers coming off the National Pass track. Work here is tourism, trades and Sydney commuting.

localities.name: Lithgow
localities.blurb: Lithgow sits at the western foot of the mountains and was built on coal, iron and the Zig Zag Railway. The small arms factory has operated in town since 1912 and is still a significant employer. Power station closures nearby have forced a hard conversation about what the valley does next.

localities.name: Oberon
localities.blurb: Oberon sits above 1100 metres in pine plantation country between Bathurst and the mountains, and it is one of the coldest towns in NSW. Softwood milling and timber processing are the main employers, with potatoes and grazing behind them. Jenolan Caves are about 30 minutes south east on a slow road.

localities.name: Sydney
localities.blurb: Sydney is the largest city in Australia, built around the harbour with the CBD running from Circular Quay down to Central. Finance, professional services, tourism and education dominate the economy. For trades the inner suburbs mean strata approvals, heritage controls and parking that costs real money on every job.

localities.name: Parramatta
localities.blurb: Parramatta is the second CBD of Sydney and sits close to the geographic centre of the metro area. Church Street, the river and a long run of tower construction define the current town. Government offices, the Westmead health precinct and a large university presence drive employment.

localities.name: Penrith
localities.blurb: Penrith sits at the foot of the Blue Mountains on the Nepean, with the whitewater stadium built for the 2000 Olympics still running. It is the service centre for the outer west and the new airport at Badgerys Creek is reshaping land use across the district. Heat matters here, with summer days regularly ten degrees above the coast.

localities.name: Liverpool
localities.blurb: Liverpool was founded in 1810 and is now one of the main centres of south west Sydney. Its hospital is one of the largest teaching hospitals in the state. Western Sydney Airport and the suburbs going up around it are the biggest change facing the district.

localities.name: Blacktown
localities.blurb: Blacktown anchors the largest local government area in NSW by population and one of the most culturally diverse in the country. Health, retail, logistics and light manufacturing are the biggest employers. Housing growth in the north west has run continuously for two decades and construction trades follow it street by street.

localities.name: Bankstown
localities.blurb: Bankstown is a centre of south west Sydney with large Vietnamese and Lebanese business communities that shape the food and retail on Chapel Road. The airport on the southern edge is one of the busiest general aviation fields in the country. Health, retail and trade based light industry are the main employers.

localities.name: Campbelltown
localities.blurb: Campbelltown is the centre of the Macarthur region at the southern edge of Sydney, with the hospital, a Western Sydney University campus and the rail line into the city. Housing estates keep extending south towards Appin. It runs hot and dry in summer, and building demand here is new homes rather than renovation.

localities.name: North Albury
localities.blurb: North Albury runs from the Waugh Road shops up to the Lavington boundary, and it is mostly postwar housing on wide blocks with the odd pocket of newer infill. Families here use the North Albury shopping strip and the sporting fields off Union Road rather than driving into the CBD. The trade work reflects the housing stock: reroofing, rewiring, drainage and bathroom rebuilds on homes built in the fifties and sixties.

localities.name: South Albury
localities.blurb: South Albury sits between the railway and the Murray flats, which is why it carries most of the light industry in town alongside its houses. Young Street and the streets off it hold workshops, wholesalers and the takeaway trade that feeds them. Because much of it is on the floodplain behind the levee, drainage, slab work and flood related repairs come up here more than anywhere else in Albury.

localities.name: East Albury
localities.blurb: East Albury climbs the hill behind the base hospital and the airport, so a large share of its working population is in health or aviation. The older streets near the hospital are tightly held and the newer estates run out towards the airport fence. Steep driveways and hillside blocks make retaining walls, tree work and stormwater the jobs local trades quote most often.

localities.name: West Albury
localities.blurb: West Albury spreads between the Murray and the Nail Can Hill range, which gives it both river frontage and bush at the back fence. It is largely residential with a primary school, a shopping strip on Kaitlers Road and heavy weekend use of the wetlands and walking tracks. Living against the range means bushfire clearing, gutter work and tree assessment are seasonal staples for trades here.

localities.name: Springdale Heights
localities.blurb: Springdale Heights is a compact residential pocket on the northern edge of Lavington, built out largely in the seventies and eighties around its primary school. There is no retail centre of its own, so the Lavington shops and the Hume Highway service strip do that job a few minutes south. Housing of that vintage keeps local trades busy with tiling, kitchen and bathroom updates, fencing and hot water replacement.
